data.title: Herpes simplex — viva
data.summary: Viral infections · 17 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Herpes simplex** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What is the causative agent and classification of HSV?**
- Herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2 — human herpesvirus 1 and 2; alpha-herpesviruses (enveloped, double-stranded DNA)
- HSV-1 mainly orolabial (now also many genital first episodes); HSV-2 mainly genital and neonatal; both stay latent in sensory ganglia (trigeminal for HSV-1, sacral for HSV-2)

**Q2. Name the 8 human herpesviruses and their diseases (very common question).**
- HHV-1 (HSV-1): orolabial herpes, keratitis, encephalitis; HHV-2 (HSV-2): genital and neonatal herpes
- HHV-3 (VZV): varicella, zoster
- HHV-4 (EBV): infectious mononucleosis, oral hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Gianotti–Crosti, hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoma
- HHV-5 (CMV): perianal ulcers in HIV, congenital infection ('blueberry muffin'), mononucleosis
- HHV-6 and 7: roseola infantum (exanthem subitum); HHV-6 reactivation in DRESS; HHV-7 linked to pityriasis rosea
- HHV-8: Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease

**Q3. Describe the pathogenesis and latency.**
- Entry through mucosa/abraded skin → replication in epidermis → retrograde axonal transport to sensory ganglion → latent (latency-associated transcripts) → reactivation with triggers travels back to skin
- Triggers: fever, UV light, menstruation, stress, trauma, immunosuppression
- Asymptomatic shedding is the main source of transmission

**Q4. Describe primary herpetic gingivostomatitis.**
- Usually HSV-1 in children 1–5 years; fever, malaise, painful vesicles that erode on gums, tongue, palate, lips; swollen bleeding gums; drooling; tender cervical nodes
- Resolves in ~2 weeks; oral acyclovir within 72–96 h shortens it

**Q5. Describe recurrent herpes labialis.**
- Prodrome of tingling/burning for hours → grouped vesicles on an erythematous base at vermilion border → pustules, crusts; heals in 7–10 days without scar
- Same site each time

**Q6. Clinical features of genital herpes.**
- First episode primary: multiple painful bilateral vesicles/erosions with fever, inguinal lymphadenopathy, dysuria; lasts 2–3 weeks; may cause aseptic meningitis, urinary retention (sacral radiculopathy)
- Recurrent: fewer, unilateral, shorter (5–10 days), less painful; HSV-2 recurs more than HSV-1
- Atypical: fissures, erythema only, in HIV — chronic deep ulcers

**Q7. What is the Tzanck smear and what does it show?**
- Scraping from the base of a fresh vesicle stained with Giemsa
- Multinucleated giant cells with nuclear moulding, margination of chromatin, and intranuclear (Cowdry A) inclusions; also acantholytic ballooned cells
- Cannot distinguish HSV from VZV; low sensitivity — PCR is now the test of choice

**Q8. Investigations for herpes?**
- PCR of vesicle fluid/swab — most sensitive and specific; typing HSV-1 vs 2
- Viral culture (declining use), direct immunofluorescence
- Type-specific serology (glycoprotein G) to detect past infection or counsel discordant couples — not for diagnosis of an active ulcer
- Screen for other STIs incl. HIV and syphilis in genital herpes

**Q9. Give the differential diagnosis of genital ulcer.**
- Painful: herpes (multiple grouped small), chancroid (ragged undermined purulent ulcer, painful suppurative bubo), traumatic, Behçet's, fixed drug eruption (recurrent same site), aphthae
- Painless: primary syphilis (indurated clean ulcer, rubbery nodes), donovanosis (beefy red, bleeds, pseudobubo), LGV (transient ulcer, then bubo with groove sign)

**Q10. Treatment of first episode genital herpes.**
- Acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 7–10 days (or 200 mg five times daily); valacyclovir 1 g twice daily 7–10 days; famciclovir 250 mg thrice daily
- Saline baths, analgesics, lidocaine gel; abstain from sex during lesions

**Q11. Treatment of recurrences and suppressive therapy.**
- Episodic: start within 24 h of prodrome — acyclovir 800 mg three times daily for 2 days, or 800 mg twice daily 5 days; valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily 3 days or 1 g daily 5 days; famciclovir 1 g twice daily for 1 day
- Suppressive (≥6 recurrences/year, severe, psychological distress, discordant partner): acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or valacyclovir 500 mg–1 g once daily; review yearly

**Q12. What is the mechanism of acyclovir? (short note)**
- Guanosine analogue phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase (so active only in infected cells) then by cellular kinases to the triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates DNA chain
- Poor oral bioavailability (~15–20%); valacyclovir prodrug gives 3–5 times higher levels
- Side effects: nausea, headache; IV — crystalline nephropathy (hydrate well), neurotoxicity in renal failure
- Resistance (thymidine kinase mutation) in immunocompromised — use foscarnet or cidofovir

**Q13. What is eczema herpeticum (Kaposi's varicelliform eruption)?**
- Widespread HSV infection on skin with an existing dermatosis (atopic dermatitis commonest, Darier's disease, pemphigus, burns, Hailey–Hailey, CTCL)
- Clusters of monomorphic punched-out haemorrhagic erosions and vesicles, fever, lymphadenopathy
- Dermatological emergency — oral/IV acyclovir; check eye involvement; risk of viraemia

**Q14. What is herpetic whitlow?**
- HSV infection of the finger — children with gingivostomatitis (thumb-sucking) and health workers; painful deep vesicles on fingertip
- Do not incise (confused with bacterial paronychia/felon)

**Q15. Name other clinical patterns of HSV infection.**
- Herpes gladiatorum (wrestlers), herpetic keratitis/keratoconjunctivitis, herpetic sycosis (beard), lumbosacral herpes
- Neonatal herpes (skin-eye-mouth, CNS, disseminated) — mother with primary genital herpes near delivery; caesarean if lesions at labour
- HSV-associated erythema multiforme (commonest cause of recurrent EM) — suppressive acyclovir prevents it
- HSV encephalitis (temporal lobe); chronic ulcerative herpes in HIV (CD4 <100) — an AIDS-defining illness if >1 month

**Q16. How do you manage herpes in pregnancy?**
- Primary infection in third trimester → highest neonatal risk: acyclovir, and caesarean section
- Recurrent herpes: suppressive acyclovir from 36 weeks; caesarean only if lesions/prodrome at labour
- Acyclovir is safe in pregnancy

**Q17. Counselling points for genital herpes?**
- Lifelong infection but recurrences become fewer with time
- Transmission can occur without lesions; condoms and suppressive therapy reduce (not eliminate) risk; inform partners
- Genital herpes increases risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV

## Quick spotter facts
- Grouped vesicles on red base, same site each time — recurrent HSV
- Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells with nuclear moulding (HSV/VZV, not distinguishable)
- Punched-out erosions on atopic skin with fever — eczema herpeticum

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections); CDC STI treatment guidelines 2021 for antiviral doses. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
